questions.enonce_markdown: **(i)** State the conditions under which the normal distribution can be used to approximate the binomial distribution.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The binomial distribution $B(n, p)$ can be approximated by the normal distribution $N(np,\ npq)$, where $q = 1 - p$, when:

1. $n$ is large (the number of trials is large, for instance $n > 30$); and
2. $p$ is close to $0.5$, so the binomial distribution is roughly symmetrical. The usual practical test is that both $np > 5$ and $nq > 5$ (some texts use 10).

Because a discrete variable is replaced by a continuous one, a **continuity correction** of $\pm 0.5$ is applied.
themes: normal approximation to the binomial distribution

questions.enonce_markdown:
**(ii)** A coin is tossed 100 times. Given that the random variable $X$ is "the number of heads obtained",

(a) Find $E(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A fair coin gives $p = 0.5$, and the 100 tosses are independent, so $X \sim B(100,\ 0.5)$.

$$E(X) = np = 100 \times 0.5 = 50$$

$$\operatorname{Var}(X) = npq = 100 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 25$$

**$E(X) = 50$, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 25$** (standard deviation $5$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the normal approximation to the binomial distribution to find, to four decimal places,

(b) $P(X < 45)$,
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $np = nq = 50 > 5$ and $n = 100$ is large, so $X$ is approximated by $W \sim N(50,\ 25)$, that is $\mu = 50$, $\sigma = 5$.

$X < 45$ means $X \le 44$ for an integer variable; the continuity correction puts the boundary at $44.5$:

$$P(X < 45) \approx P(W < 44.5) = P\!\left(Z < \frac{44.5 - 50}{5}\right) = P(Z < -1.1) = 1 - \Phi(1.1)$$

From the tables $\Phi(1.1) = 0.8643$, so

$$P(X < 45) = 1 - 0.8643 = 0.1357$$

**$P(X < 45) \approx 0.1357$.**
themes: normal approximation to the binomial distribution
